The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Summary of 2001 Political Manifesto

This manifesto outlines policy proposals across multiple areas with stated themes of personal liberty, fairness, and fiscal transparency.

## Healthcare
The document proposes reducing NHS waiting times through recruiting 27,500 additional nurses, 4,600 doctors, and 10,250 allied health professionals over five years. It advocates providing 10,000 extra hospital beds, pay increases for lower-paid NHS staff, and free dental and eye checks. A key commitment is state funding for long-term personal care costs, already implemented in Scotland. The manifesto supports reducing bureaucratic targets and giving medical professionals greater clinical autonomy.

## Education
Education proposals include reducing primary school class sizes to an average of 25 pupils for ages 5-11, recruiting 5,000 additional secondary teachers, and increasing funding for books and equipment. The manifesto commits to abolishing university tuition fees UK-wide, restoring maintenance grants for poorer students, and replacing performance-related pay with professional development-linked salary increases. These measures would be funded through a one penny increase on basic income tax.

## Criminal Justice
Policing proposals include 6,000 additional officers, 2,000 part-time community officers, and a Community Safety Force. The manifesto emphasises crime prevention over prison expansion, proposing rehabilitation programmes and skills training for prisoners. It supports maintaining jury trial rights and opposes mandatory sentencing except for minor offences. A Standing Royal Commission would review drug policy.

## Transport
Transport proposals include free off-peak local bus travel for pensioners and disabled people, abolishing vehicle tax for low-emission cars, and reforming railway regulation. The manifesto opposes air traffic control privatisation and supports freight transfer to rail and waterways.

## Welfare and Pensions
Pension increases of £5-15 weekly for single pensioners are proposed, funded by a 50% tax rate on income exceeding £100,000. The manifesto supports annual minimum wage reviews, restored benefits for young people, and extended winter fuel payments to severely disabled individuals.

## Constitutional Reform
Proposals include electoral reform through the AV+ system with a referendum, replacing the House of Lords with an elected Senate, strengthening regional devolution, and introducing local income tax to replace Council Tax. The voting age would be lowered to 16.

## Civil Liberties
The manifesto proposes an Equality Act covering discrimination on all grounds, asylum system reform including abolishing vouchers, strengthened freedom of information legislation, and civil partnership registration.

## European and International Policy
European policy supports EU enlargement, institutional reform, and euro membership subject to referendum. Defence spending would be maintained while arms export subsidies would end. The manifesto commits to the 0.7% GDP overseas aid target.

## Environment
Environmental proposals include 10% renewable energy by 2010, phasing out nuclear power, household recycling collection, a carbon tax replacing the Climate Change Levy, and GM crop moratorium until 2004.

## Economic Policy
Fiscal proposals include income tax increases for education funding, a 50% rate on high earners, and Capital Gains Tax reform. Long-term goals include eliminating income tax for the lowest earners and annual citizen tax statements.

# Summary of 2001 UK General Election Manifesto

This manifesto presents a comprehensive policy programme centred on the theme of returning power and responsibility to individuals, families, and local communities rather than centralising control within government.

## Family and Education

The document proposes tax reductions for families with young children, including increased child tax credits and allowances for married couples with children under 11. Education reforms focus on granting greater autonomy to schools, allowing headteachers control over admissions, staffing, and discipline. The manifesto advocates for enabling successful schools to expand, permitting new schools to be established by faith groups and charitable foundations, and giving parents rights to trigger inspections of underperforming schools. Student loan repayment thresholds would be raised, and university endowment funds would be created to reduce dependence on state funding.

## Law and Order

The manifesto commits to increasing police numbers and reducing bureaucratic burdens on officers. Proposals include secure training centres for persistent young offenders, mandatory prison sentences for those selling drugs to minors, and honest sentencing where criminals serve the full term given by courts. Victims would receive improved communication from police and prosecutors, with reforms to self-defence laws.

## Economic Policy

Economic proposals include reducing the overall tax burden through targeted cuts for families, pensioners, and motorists, including a 6p per litre reduction in fuel tax. The manifesto commits to keeping the pound sterling and maintaining monetary independence. A deregulation agenda would require government departments to reduce regulatory burdens annually, with small businesses exempt from certain regulations.

## Healthcare

Healthcare reforms would remove political interference from clinical decisions, introduce maximum waiting times based on medical need, and allow patients to choose their hospital. The manifesto proposes restoring authority to ward sisters and matrons while removing tax penalties on private medical insurance.

## Pensions and Elderly Care

Pensioners would benefit from increased tax allowances, removing one million from income tax entirely. The basic pension would increase, with additional amounts for those over 75. The manifesto proposes abolishing compulsory annuity purchases at age 75 and allowing pension fund inheritance.

## Local Government and Rural Affairs

The manifesto advocates abolishing regional development agencies, strengthening local councils, and protecting green spaces. Rural communities would receive support through reduced business rates for local services and fuel tax relief. Recovery measures address the ongoing agricultural crisis.

## Constitutional Matters

Proposed reforms include restricting voting on England-only matters to English MPs, strengthening parliamentary scrutiny, and opposing further transfers of power to European institutions while supporting a more flexible European Union structure.
